speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This Code would not have been possible without the leadership, efforts and contributions of the trade associations and chambers (TACs) from the retail and property sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: So, on behalf of the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and on behalf of the Government, I want to say a big thank you to the various trade associations and industry groups that came together to develop this Code and chart a new and fair future for the leasing of retail premises.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: And these include the Singapore Business Federation (SBF), Restaurant Association of Singapore (RAS), SG Tenants United for Fairness (SGTUFF), Singapore Retail Association (SRA), Association of Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (ASME), the Real Estate Developers' Association of Singapore (REDAS) and the REIT Association of Singapore (REITAS).

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: They sought to promote fair and balanced leasing negotiations by setting out a framework for industry norms on tenancy practices and terms, which are now spelt out in the Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: After the Code was launched, a Fair Tenancy Industry Committee was formed in May 2021 to act as custodian of the Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: We commend the industry and the leaders for their courage and tenacity in charting the path forward towards fair leasing practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: In fact, around the table, the stakeholders have shown tremendous maturity and resilience in their discussions as well as admirable willingness to give and take, as they worked towards achieving the common goal for the retail sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This spirit of trust and strong partnership between tenants and landlords was forged in the early days of the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: For example, when retailers had to pivot to e-commerce channels, if you remember, back in the circuit breaker days, to keep their businesses afloat, landlords, such as CapitaLand, stepped up by launching the eCapitaMall platform to help their tenants sell their products or services online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: CapitaLand also provided marketing and promotional assistance to enhance the e-commerce capabilities of its traditional retailers on the e-mall.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This innovative move and collaboration helped CapitaLand and their tenants to continue to generate revenue during the challenging circuit breaker period – generating revenue even as there were restrictions on dining in and other safe management measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: It is with this spirit of partnership between the tenants and the landlords that the Code was established.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: In the larger scheme of things, the Code not only benefits tenants and landlords but also supports a vibrant and healthy lifestyle sector and contributes to our tourism industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: At this point, allow me to highlight how the Code is expected to benefit the industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The Code provides tenants and landlords with greater clarity on industry norms for key terms in retail lease agreements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This makes the negotiation process more transparent for both parties and addresses tenants' concerns over imbalances in bargaining power.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Since the Code's introduction on 1 June 2021, the Government has been a lead adopter, with all Government landlords voluntarily adopting the Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: In addition, nine major private sector landlords have also adopted the Code voluntarily since June 2021.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: These early movers have found the Code helpful for their lease negotiations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: In my various engagements with many tenants and landlords, their overall feedback has been positive and constructive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: For example, in the last few weeks, there was one landlord representative who recently shared with us that adopting the Code has made negotiations with tenants simpler and swifter, simply because both parties signing the agreement were Code-compliant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: And this, in fact, has helped the landlord to establish good relationships with tenants and vice versa.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Tenant representatives also shared that the Code has helped to level the playing field somewhat and enabled parties to find more common ground in lease negotiations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: We expect the Code to be a "living document" that continues to evolve based on the feedback and suggestions from the industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: As custodian of the Code, the FTIC will update the Code as necessary to ensure its continued relevance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Deviations from selected leasing principles are permitted with mutual consent by tenants and landlords.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This keeps the Code from being overly restrictive and this will allow for the usual commercial negotiations and considerations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The Bill also requires tenants and landlords to make declarations of some of the deviations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The current Committee has made the process of submitting declarations an easy one via its website and this will continue to be the mode of submission after the Bill is passed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: I wish to assure the House that both the mediation and the adjudication processes will be kept low-cost and expedient.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The Government thanks the efforts of the Fair Tenancy Pro Tem Committee and the current Committee and welcomes the FTIC in continuing the role of custodian of the Code under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: We would also like to express our appreciation to the apex business chamber in Singapore, SBF, for agreeing to take on the role of secretariat to FTIC.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The Bill will apply to all leases of retail premises, or extensions and renewals of such lease, with a tenure of one year or more.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Under the Bill, retail premises are those that are used primarily for the retail sale of goods or the supply of services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This includes businesses, such as eateries, restaurants, supermarkets, clinics, pet shops, walk-in bank branches, tuition centres, cinemas and gyms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: In general, businesses in the shopping malls are also covered under the Bill, unless the premises are mainly used for backend office functions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: On the other hand, premises used primarily for conducting administrative work in connection with the supply of services are not covered under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Likewise, industrial, office and residential spaces are excluded unless the space is tenanted to a shop supplying retail goods or services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: For example, a mini-mart that operates in an office or industrial building will be covered under the Bill, while the rest of the building that is used as office spaces or for industrial activities will not be covered.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: We are greatly heartened that many major landlords have already adopted the Code since it was established two years ago.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Together, they make up a sizeable proportion of all retail premises in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: To provide additional time for other landlords to come on board, the Bill will take effect about six months from now, in early February 2024.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: All new lease agreements, extensions or renewals of lease agreements, signed on or after this commencement date, will be covered by the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: It has also shown that with unity, we can overcome adversity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This Bill was forged from the resilience and determination of tenants and landlords to turn their difficulties into opportunities for partnership and success.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: I trust that the industry will continue to uphold this exemplary spirit of cooperation between tenants and landlords in our journey ahead.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: As we strive to build on this firm foundation of partnership and trust, we seek to create a robust and thriving economy that continues to provide good jobs and a bright future for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is especially so for businesses in the retail sector, both large and small, as rental of premises forms a significant part of business cost.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This fact was acutely felt when retail businesses were heavily impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic when the ability to operate from their retail premises had to be restricted or even halted.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Likewise for landlords, both large and smaller landlords, as rent is the source of income.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While I do agree that the balance of power does tend to favour landlords, as we give due consideration for the needs of retail businesses, we have to take a win-win approach for both landlords and tenants.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If this is achieved, retail businesses can have fair and predictable rents and terms and conditions to allow them to operate in a highly competitive market while landlords can benefit from the occupancy and continue to invest in the quality of their properties and marketing programmes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am supportive and agree that it is timely to move ahead with legislation and compliance with the Code.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One, the Code enables a fair and balanced lease negotiation process benefiting both landlords and tenants.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It sets out clear leasing guidelines and negotiation principles for landlords and tenants of Qualifying Retail Premises in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is an effort by industry comprising landlord and tenants, who are the key stakeholders, and supported by the Government, industry experts and academia.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is important as it provides clarity on the terms in the lease agreement, easing the leasing negotiation process for landlords and, more importantly, for tenants, the Code addresses key concerns over an imbalance in bargaining power.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The second reason is that there has been positive voluntary adoption of the Code.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: After the release of the Code in 2021, it is positive that over the last two years, major industry landlords and all Government landlords have voluntarily adopted the Code.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, that is a positive sign because, clearly, the Code is fair and for both parties.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Third, support in place for ease of compliance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: FTIC has taken several actions to ease compliance for landlords and tenants with the launch of a sample lease agreement template and a portal to facilitate joint reporting by landlord and tenants on deviations and FTIC has also developed a checklist for lease negotiations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Fourth, there has also been very active engagement with industry stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Through outreach and briefing sessions with industry stakeholders, which included the TACs, the Law Society and real estate agencies, FTIC has received feedback and has updated the Code.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Government has conducted industry and public consultation on key provisions in 2022.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, before I conclude, I would like to say that while we recognise the benefits and should go ahead with legislation, we should not expect legislation to be the panacea for all issues.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Lease agreements are between two parties, landlord and tenants.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Ultimately, as in every good relationship, we must adopt a win-win approach, one that is fair and predictable for the tenant so that he or she can focus on growing the business, while aligned to market conditions so that landlords can continue to make investments to maintain the property and promote vibrancy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am glad that the Minister of State has just reassured us that FTIC will continue to review and engage landlords and tenants to obtain feedback and, with the appropriate approvals, update the Code and this is important to ensure its relevance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, it is often also a relationship which is hugely imbalanced, with landlords having a significant advantage over tenants when it comes to lease negotiations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is this power imbalance which we should strive to address and ensure a more level playing field for tenants, especially small and medium enterprises (SMEs), who are beholden to landlords, and with rents being a critical overhead cost for retailers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As what some retailers would say, "We are merely working for the landlord”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The power disparity and helplessness of tenants came to the fore in recent years as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, where mandatory lockdowns and safe-distancing measures put the retail landscape under significant strain.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, the silver lining, of course, was the formation of self-help groups, such as the Singapore Tenants United for Fairness (SGTUFF), the formation of the Fair Tenancy Pro Tem Committee and, eventually, the Code of Conduct for Leasing of Retail Premises and the legislation we see today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To this end, I am supportive of the Bill in its efforts to address certain pain points and unfair leasing terms and conditions that used to be prevalent in the retail landscape.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, however, I will speak broadly on areas for improvements, particularly as they relate to data availability and transparency, which, in my view, are the core issues that need to be addressed in enabling a more diverse, inclusive and level playing field for the sustainability of our retail landscape.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One way that landlords could wield a disproportionate amount of power at the negotiating table is by exploiting the information disparity between them and the tenants.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This enables them to command higher rents during lease negotiations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While clauses 5 and 6 of the Bill codify the leasing principles set out in the Code of Conduct for the Leasing of Retail Premises in Singapore, the current code and, hence, legislation, does not include data transparency guidelines as a requirement for all qualifying leases.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, there is much room for improvement here, especially when I believe the majority of rents today do not incorporate GTO rent arrangements and, hence, this leasing principle may not apply to many leases in practice.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Retailers which The Business Times spoke to for an article dated 19 July 2023 further mentioned that data, such as fine-grained footfall and rental data, would be useful for tenants during lease negotiations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, they noted that the sales data provided by landlords should be broken down by floor and sub-category as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In accounting, there is a concept called "decision usefulness" which comes to my mind; without granular data, the information provided by landlords would be neither useful nor relevant for tenants or potential tenants.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, if one is a small F&B kiosk operator on the highest floor of a shopping mall, of what use is the total F&B sales for the entire mall if the McDonald's outlet on the ground floor is doing brisk business and likely dominates the consolidated sales figures?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Will the Minister consider providing for more fine-grained data to be presented and at a higher frequency versus the current bi-annual basis?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, lease agreements may contain confidentiality clauses within contracts, prohibiting tenants from sharing information regarding their lease agreements, including rental rates, with their counterparts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Landlords, however, could have access to comprehensive data from their tenant’s Point-of-Sales (POS) systems, be it across multiple tenants from within the same mall, or the same tenant across different malls, thus enabling them to maximise potential rents and, hence, occupancy costs from the perspective of tenants, without causing them to vacate their space.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the new Bill certainly helps to reduce the power differential between landlords and tenants, enhancing data transparency would certainly help to further reduce this gap.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe the data transparency guidelines set out in the Code should be mandated under the new legislation, rather than applying only to landlords who collect sales data from tenants as part of the GRO rent structure.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To take it one step further to truly enable fair and equal access to information for landlords and tenants alike, I hope that the Government would also consider launching a public rental information database, similar to that mooted by the Fair Tenancy Framework Industry Committee back in 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Not only would such information benefit tenants, especially SME tenants, who may not have the ability to compare rents and key retail metrics across locations, smaller landlords would also benefit from the ability to better position their mall in a market dominated by key players.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To use an example which, arguably, is not related to a shopping mall, if you look at the recent concerns over the Geylang Serai Ramadan Bazaar, for example, while many have expressed concerns over high rental costs, especially for certain food types, in my mind, it is the uncertainty in the ability to make enough revenue to cover rents and other costs that weighs heavily on tenants’ minds throughout the tenure of the bazaar.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, past sales information, footfall and other related metrics provided would then help in this decision-making.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I understand that there are various retail indices being compiled by the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA), the overall market index may not accurately reflect the nuances of the different geographical submarkets and, certainly, not the individual shopping malls.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Besides enhancing data and information transparency, I believe efforts should also be put into ensuring that tenants are better informed when negotiating their leases and signing the lease agreement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: An adjacent point worth considering is whether such a code of conduct can also be extended to non-retail leases, to other commercial leases, such as those for offices or even those for industrial and business park spaces.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: SME tenants that are the beneficiaries of the retail code of conduct could also benefit from fairer and more balanced lease negotiations between landlords and tenants of workspaces.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given that significant effort had already been put in by various parties to refine the retail code of conduct, it would be worthwhile, in my view, to look into extending this to other commercial and industrial sectors.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A quick scroll through the tenant directories of the numerous malls that populate our island shows that the same chain stores and eateries repeatedly pop up.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As someone who frequently patronises McDonald's and Uniqlo, I can understand why these retailers are doing so well and why many malls would want these ubiquitous names as anchor tenants for their malls.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, such brand-name tenants or other international F&B or fashion retailers could potentially also afford higher rents as opposed to the local SMEs, thus enabling landlords to command higher rentals at their malls and thereby uplifting the valuations of their properties.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This could, however, potentially have a stifling and crowding out impact on our local SME and retail scene.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, the shopping mall, of which many populate our island, forms a key backdrop to the everyday experiences and lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Fostering an environment that encourages our smaller retailers to flourish could bring greater vibrancy and character to these places and Singapore as a whole.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.18 pm until 3.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It seeks to level the playing field between landlords and tenants of retail premises in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill is a step in the right direction and I commend the Government for this.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Landlords can also no longer include exclusivity clauses that restrict tenants from opening another outlet within a certain radius unless there is mutual agreement between the tenant and landlord.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An affordable dispute resolution process will also be set up to mediate disputes between tenants and landlords.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All these will strengthen SMEs in the retail and F&B sectors in Singapore, which, for too long, had been at the mercy of landlords.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For many years, SME tenants have borne the brunt of unfair leasing practices by landlords who have taken advantage of them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, there were many cases of landlords refusing to reduce the rent while their tenants were in dire straits or failing to pass down savings from property tax rebates to their tenants.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill is, therefore, an encouraging first step to create fairer and more equitable leasing practices in the retail sector.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague Ms Hazel Poa and I have spoken in this House many times before about the need to curb excessive property speculation and rein in property prices and rental in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, during the housing debate in February this year, I said, "The more important property investment and speculation become in an economy, the more likely that economy will become less competitive because property speculation and rent seeking are easier and better alternatives to innovation and entrepreneurship." This also means that the total factor productivity of Singapore will remain low – an issue which we have debated during the National Productivity Fund (Amendment) Bill just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I was talking about residential property previously, the same thing applies to the commercial property market in Singapore, where we also see the emergence of a rentier economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The power balance has always been tilted in favour of landlords because there is a limited pool of landlords that tenants in the retail sector can choose their rent from, given the many shopping malls that are now owned by commercial real estate investment trusts (REITs).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For many years, these big institutional landlords have had the market power to extract rent from tenants through unfair rent structures, such as charging tenants a base rent or a percentage of gross sales, whichever is higher.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This rent computation structure means that landlords enjoy the good times as rent increases in tandem with sales and are still protected during bad times as tenants must continue to pay the base rent to the landlords.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even large retail and F&B chains must play by these rules, not to mention SMEs in the retail sector.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such rental computation structures sap the vitality of the retail and F&B sectors in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The House should note that even under the proposed legislation, landlords are still allowed to impose such rental computation structures provided there is mutual agreement between the landlord and tenant.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We call on the Government to consider asserting its influence and encourage FTIC to outlaw such rental computation structures altogether in the next iteration of the code of conduct.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, more work needs to be done to reduce rent seeking in the retail sector in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore needs more innovation and entrepreneurial spirit to continue competing effectively with the rest of the world in the Information Age.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such innovation and entrepreneurship are unlikely to be forthcoming if the business environment in Singapore favours rent-seeking property owners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: High rents also limit wage growth for local workers and perpetuate the need to bring in cheaper foreign workers in order to maintain profit margins for entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Small business owners in Singapore face a multitude of challenges, such as the rising costs of goods, utilities and labour, which have not abated since the pandemic ended.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A reset of our current policies is needed to create an environment that is more favourable for small businesses to ensure that jobs are created and our economy remains vibrant for many years to come.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore does not need an economy with high property prices and high rents but a dearth of innovation and creativity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Addressing the power imbalance between retail landlords and tenants is only a small step in that direction.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Bill aims to create a fairer and more equitable industry overall and, as a result, fosters sustainable growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we delve into the Bill's intricacies, some important concerns and suggestions come to light.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If so, does the Bill mandate landlords to provide detailed breakdowns of service charges and A&P spending?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Transparency in these matters will ensure fair dealings and build trust among all parties.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, landlords may face mounting cost pressures for third-party services like cleaning and lift maintenance, which may not align with tenancy terms.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This situation might tempt landlords to price in a buffer or front load service charge costs, potentially affecting tenants' financial burdens.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Conversely, the Bill should also address the concern of landlords backloading an increase of service costs during lease renewals to recover the difference from the initial term.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such practices would contradict the principle of no overall gross rent increase.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, there is a risk of under-accounting or an under-declaration of rent revenue due to price-in buffers of the service charge component.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This could lead to reduced stamp duty collections, impacting Government revenue.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, with regard to material adverse changes, this Bill compels parties to renegotiate the lease agreement when the tenant is prevented, obstructed or hindered from performing its typical business activity at the leased premises due to events beyond their control.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Does the Bill provide clear guidelines and principles for conducting these renegotiations, ensuring equitable outcomes for both parties involved?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During the challenging times of the COVID-19 pandemic, certain rent waivers provided by the Government were not efficiently passed through to tenants, requiring substantial efforts from relevant authorities to ensure proper implementation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In exigent situations like these, having agreed on guidelines and principles for renegotiations becomes even more critical.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, regarding deviations in leasing principles, the Bill allows for leasing principle deviations wherein landlords and tenants can mutually agree to deviate from the principles.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To address non-compliance by errant landlords, what regulatory powers and levers are vested in the Government or the FTIC?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Further, how will the FTIC be informed if a landlord has filed a deviation or not, ensuring proper oversight and compliance with the leasing principles?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourth, with regard to cost, this Bill includes essential prohibitions and norms.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Landlords are mandated to pass through electricity costs without any mark-up or price discrimination.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This move aims to shield SMEs from additional burdens and foster a more equitable business environment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, I have received feedback from SMEs which shared that they are being charged for additional miscellaneous costs, such as "meter reading fees", in addition to electricity charges.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Tenants are now being charged monthly recurring charges, such as meter readings, tenant management charges and meter leasing fees.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Due to advances in digital metering technologies, recurring charges for tenant management charges and meter readings are not justified.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this regard, the following points need further clarification.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Two, with regard to the meter leasing fees, can tenants have the option to purchase the meter instead of being bound by leasing arrangements?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Three, can the Bill specify specific technology adoption, such as digital meters, which do not require manual or physical on-site meter readings?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will not only increase overall productivity but also support Singapore's Green Plan 2030, empowering tenants with real-time data on power usage and insights to reduce energy consumption.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Four, do tenants have the option to enter into direct purchase agreements with electricity retailers?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This provision would grant tenants more flexibility in managing their electricity costs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we continue to finetune the Lease Agreement Bill, addressing these crucial points regarding (a) A&P and Service charges; (b) clear guidelines and principles for conducting re-negotiations during adverse situations; (c) deviations of leasing principles, its remedies and oversight; and (d) clarifications on electricity charges will contribute to establishing a more transparent framework for both landlords and tenants.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill's significance lies in its commitment to fostering win-win outcomes and promoting compromise, ensuring a conducive environment for sustainable growth for our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Let us continue to engage in constructive discussions to achieve win-win outcomes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Its title is the Lease Agreements for Retail Premises Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Its spirit, though, is a deep rethinking of the moral limits of markets.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Markets in Singapore, as in almost every country in the world, are created not only by supply and demand but by the laws that regulate them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Being one of the most competitive countries in the world, Singapore takes a light touch towards constraining the freedoms of markets.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And most of the time, this has been the case, both because of the need for efficiency and the belief in the wise decisions of a relatively unfettered marketplace.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But let us make no bones that, in Singapore, a nation founded on the back of a socialist political philosophy, the market bends for the public good.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And through this Bill, the Government has demonstrated that it is not shackled by the positions it took in the past and is willing to constantly review its policies to ensure that they address the needs of our people and enterprises.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I specifically highlighted landlords of retail malls, particularly the REITs, as one category of dominant players.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech, I recounted how a “demolition clause”, which is a clause that allows a landlord to pre-terminate a lease with a tenant on the basis that it has decided to undertake renovation work without any compensation to the tenant, works unfairly against many tenants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These tenants would have invariably incurred capital expenses to fit out the premises and they were left to bear the loss themselves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This does not appear to be a fair sharing of business risks.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also highlighted other onerous clauses imposed by landlords in my speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This asymmetry adds insult to injury when we remember that tenants are small businesses and landlords are owners of large assets.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I advocated those small businesses to be provided with statutory protection in Singapore beyond the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I shared the examples of small business protection modes in the UK, Hong Kong, the US, Germany and Australia.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She also said: “enacting such legislation in Singapore can cause market distortion and, eventually, market inefficiency, to the detriment of all”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She also said to the effect that an answer to what constitutes a fair dealing is not something that is always clear-cut because different parties may have different views.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I listened to the hon Minister of State and I noted that the pandemic posed to be a catalyst for this change.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And this is a great example of how one turns crisis into opportunity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It recognises that free market principles are not the holy grail of public policy, that these principles must bend to larger principles of public life.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill recognises that landlords and tenants stand shoulder to shoulder, both with legitimate interests.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister of State referred to the relationship as a symbiotic relationship.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They share a mutual goal of collaboration to ensure that Singapore continues to have vibrant and competitive retail, F&B and lifestyle sectors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The beauty of this Code is that it is put up by a Committee representing both the interests of the landlords and tenants and consists also of neutral parties, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The expectation is that the Committee can provide holistic guidance on what constitutes fair practices in the context of retail lease agreements.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Earlier, just before the break, the hon Member Mr Louis Chua had suggested that perhaps the Government should consider more data transparency guidelines in favour of tenants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On its own, it is not a controversial point, but my suggestion is this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have this committee that is supposed to come to a consensus, a collective action plan.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In that regard, one would have to not just look at specific issues, but really the net picture.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And in that regard, we must always take a give-and-take approach.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, when we take issues or advocate issues pertaining to the tenants, we must also consider what are the landlords’ issues and then we can come to a consensus and, hopefully, we can move forward.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Non-Constituency Member of Parliament Mr Leong Mun Wai had advocated some form of low-rent control.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have been in legal practice long enough to remember the spectre of the Rent Control Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In those days, because of the Rent Control Act, there was no real investment by the landlords on their premises, leading to dilapidated buildings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And in the end, Singapore suffers because small Singapore would require a high utility of our land.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, what is fair in the circumstances would have to be determined by the market and now, we have this framework in terms of a committee and we need to take a consensual approach to deal with all these issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A plain reading of the Code will show that the focus is really to protect the small tenant and not the big landlord.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I welcome the Government’s decision to intervene for the small tenant in the retail sector.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It also makes business sense in the long term, because otherwise, we would see a hollowing out of SMEs, which are representative of our nation’s entrepreneurial spirit, within the retail sector.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is a third principle that this Bill makes provisions for, but, in my view, it has not gone far enough.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a point that the hon Member Mr Louis Chua also made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also wish to draw attention to contracts made by small businesses with other dominant players, such as telcos and utility services providers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Thankfully, where the dominant players are regulated, I see an ability on the part of the regulators to reign in unfair practices and ensure fair dealing outcomes through the exercise of their regulatory powers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is done, for example, by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) which issued Fair Dealing Guidelines in 2013.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I suggested in my 2018 speech that other regulators follow suit.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What would be useful, in particular, is to ensure that the contracts issued by dominant players, which are regulated, are reviewed for compliance with such guidelines, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, there should be no gap between regulation and contract.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This dispute is to be resolved through mediation first.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If mediation does not work, then it is proposed that it be dealt with by an adjudicator who will have the power to not just determine whether there is a non-compliance with a leasing principle but also to deal with the issue of compensation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In turn, the authorised dispute resolution body must maintain a panel of mediators and adjudicators.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My first question is what are the proposed qualifications of the mediators and adjudicators?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, why is it felt that the appointments of the mediators and adjudicators should not be done directly by the hon Minister?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My next question concerns the power of the adjudicator.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In such a case, the adjudicator may vary the lease agreement to correct the non-compliance or he may order compensation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, may I ask what are the principles upon which the adjudicator is to calculate compensation?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Is it based on the law governing damages for breach of contract?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Or can the adjudicator decide on compensation in accordance with his own views of what is just and equitable in the circumstances?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How would he deal with clauses in the lease agreements that attempt to exclude or limit liability for compensation?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Moving on, it is proposed in clause 13 of the Bill that where there are any proceedings before a Court in respect of a matter that is subject of Part 4 of this Bill, the Court may order a stay of proceedings on terms that it sees fit.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If the legislative intent is to ensure that the adjudicator, and not the Court, handles all complaints of non-compliance with leasing principles, would it not be better to provide that the Court must grant a stay, say for limited circumstances, instead of making it discretionary?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for the hon Minister’s clarification on this matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If, indeed, it is intended that the Court be vested with a discretion, may I ask the hon Minister of State what factors must the Court weigh in determining whether or not to grant a stay, having regard to the legislative objective of this Bill?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also seek a clarification on the ambit of clause 28 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It allows a party to raise challenges to the lease agreement on the basis of whether or not it complies with the proposed Act in separate Court, arbitral tribunal or other dispute resolution proceeding.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At first glance, it seems to be that clause 28 may not be congruent with the legislative intent to channel disputes arising from the Act to the adjudicator.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under sub-clause (5), a non-exclusive list of grounds is provided for the purpose of setting aside the order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In essence, the grounds are illegality and palpable injustice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If that is the case, would the hon Minister of State please clarify the reason for doing so?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I ask this also bearing in mind that the adjudicator may have to apply the law governing contracts as determined by the Courts to issues at hand, for example, compensation and dealing with the enforceability of exclusion and indemnity clauses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Since what constitutes such law are matters within the province of the Courts, I would have thought that there should be recourse to the Court system as a matter of right.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: An alternative option is to allow for an appeal if it raises an issue of law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It gives life to everything I had imagined in my Adjournment Motion five years ago.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I should also thank the Minister for Trade and Industry, who is here as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To my colleagues in this House, may I be allowed to share that in Parliamentary life, sometimes, time is the secret ingredient.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Surely, this is a very good deal in the marketplace of ideas.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, you have a clarification for Mr Murali?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Perhaps Member Murali is too happy with this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If I hear correctly, he mentioned that I recommended rent control in my speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I did not assert that the hon Member Mr Leong sought rent control.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I was in legal practice long enough to remember the Rent Control Act, which was subsequently abolished.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And I recall that where Rent Control Act applies, buildings become dilapidated because landlords have no incentive to invest in these buildings and making it tenantable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And in the end, Singaporeans suffer, because there is no utility that arises from the use of land.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What you have said is actually a very dangerous inference into what I say.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think I would ask you to retract what you have said.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because I have actually agreed with this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And the direction that the Government has taken in this Bill, I totally agree with.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is something that is quite rare, actually, that I agree with the direction of the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I did not say that I am asking for lower rents.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am just saying that, in general, we should not encourage too much property speculation and we should not encourage a rent-seeking economy or society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, you should not bring what I said in my speech to that conclusion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is very unfair for the inference that you have made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, in the context of that, it is always a give and take.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And, to advocate for specific issues for one party may be good in Courts of law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But within the framework that is being proposed in this Bill, that is anathema – because the whole idea here is to have a collaborative, consensual approach; be it in relation to rent or even in relation to sharing of data.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Speaker, Sir, I think that explanation is still not enough.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You must be very clear that I did not say that I am advocating rent control.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because what you are trying to say is actually, sorry, it is actually quite similar to what the Government has always been saying with regard to what I recommend in this House.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When I talk about we should not encourage too much property speculation; with this Bill, we can have more control over the big property landlord, you say I am advocating, you say what I am saying is going to lead to rent control.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Just like whenever I said about protecting the jobs of Singaporeans, the Government accused —

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I had just now already, in my first clarification, stated that I did not say that the hon Member Mr Leong advocated rent control.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And against that clarification, why is the hon Member still maintaining that I said he advocated rent control?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: From what I say, I do not like the inference that he has made, that I am trying to recommend pushing down the rent and towards the direction of rent control and, as a result, it will affect the desire, the motivation of the landlords in Singapore to make further investment in property and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think this is too much of inference.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And I am trying to quote that what I say, for example, in jobs, the Government tried to label me as xenophobic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When I talk about lower housing prices, the Government said I am trying to raid the reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This is the same pattern of what the Member Mr Murali is trying to do here, in my opinion.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Murali, would you like to respond to that again?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, with great respect, I fail to see how I am accused of taking his speech out of tangent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But in any event, the record would prove what I said and, therefore, apart from these comments, I do not wish to take this any further.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think what both Mr Murali and Mr Leong have said will be recorded clearly in the Hansard.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I would like to propose that we move on from here.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Both Mr Leong and Mr Murali have clarified.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Okay, Mr Leong, I will allow one last clarification.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I want to clarify here, I never in my speech, mentioned I am asking for lower rent.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, I think that point has been clarified.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It will all be recorded – what you said and what Mr Murali said.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Speaker, Sir, so, can I confirm that if afterwards we have confirmed that I did not say that I am asking for lower rent, I am just talking of general approach, Member Murali will apologise to me and correct his statement?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Member Murali, can I ask whether you will commit to that?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Of course, Mr Leong is entitled to his views and I hope that he respects that I am entitled to my views as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I have already offered that whatever we have said is recorded in Hansard and we stand by what we say.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And I think whatever that we do, our conduct in all these things, would have to be something that would flow from there.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, I am not going to make any commitment.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As I have said, Mr Murali Pillai has clarified, as well as Mr Leong, you have also clarified what you have said.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The introduction of the Lease Agreements for Retail Premises Bill is timely.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Schemes, such as the Self-Employed Person Income Relief Scheme, which the NTUC had assisted the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) to administer, gave some respite to many self-employed business owners.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Post-pandemic, businesses are starting to find their footing.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Others still choose to operate as retail tenants.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They include enrichment centres, gyms and photography studios.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Shop rental is a significant operating cost to self-employed business owners.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To move towards fairer rent structures and profit-sharing clauses in the lease agreements, business owners suggest guidance.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This guidance could be from the Government and market leaders.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, sudden and drastic increase in rental cost destabilises small businesses.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This left many small businesses in the deep end.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Landlords cited inflation, higher expenses and opportunity costs to justify rental hikes.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many had depleted their savings during COVID-19 and were in a state of financial flux.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Self-employed businesses located in non-retail commercial properties also shared this concern.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, a vibrant business ecosystem encourages a variety of business forms to co-exist.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Even so, what must change for small businesses to co-exist with big tenants with deep pockets?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For example, landlords could calibrate rental adjustments over a longer period.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This would allow small businesses time to adjust their business models.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Landlords could also share how they derived various costs like base rent.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This would help tenants to appreciate the extent economic factors impact retail rents and provide them with lead time to communicate fee increases with customers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Third, labour is often the next most significant operating cost following rental.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, business owners might shift towards flexible labour to counter higher rental costs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, staffing might consist of short-term contracts and gig-based freelancing arrangements.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: While this increases business flexibility, it is at the expense of worker income security.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: If rent remains an uncertainty for business owners, "flexibilisation" of employment could become more appealing.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This is an area of concern as worker precariousness cannot be an outcome of business survival.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Emerging from the pandemic, small businesses have been bracing themselves for various headwinds.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It helps to balance the bargaining power between landlords and retail tenants.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Self-employed business owners are aware of their vulnerabilities in a volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous (VUCA) environment.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They thus look to the Government and market leaders to guide fair play and practices.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This is important to the development of a sustainable and vibrant business ecosystem – one where self-employed business owners and their workforce can thrive and where consumers can benefit from the diversity and affordability of goods and services.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the suggestion, the Bill gives assurance to small businesses.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: That is the difference between someone who can speak from a small device as compared to me with a big device.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I call the next Member, I would just like to remind all Members of what I said right at the start of the Sitting yesterday, which is, by all means, speak with passion, speak with conviction.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But there is no need, I again remind Members that there is no need to bang on the rostrum or things of that sort.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I would hate to give reminders every now and then.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Code was first released by FTIC in 2021.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill takes the important step of codifying the Code.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the effect of non-compliance with the Code of Conduct.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State clarify if non-compliance with the leasing principles that is not a permitted deviation will mean that the non-compliant term is void?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State also clarify if there are any situations where non-compliance with the leasing principles that is not a permitted deviation will void the entire lease?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These clarifications will help parties clearly understand the legal consequences of non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In situations where a non-compliant term or the entire lease is void, can the Minister of State clarify how the Court should determine what sums are due to parties?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on modifications to the Codes and the Schedules.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The modifications do not require approval of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While there should be flexibility, transparency and certainty for businesses are also important.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share how frequently the Code of Conduct will be modified?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State also elaborate on the criteria and considerations for modifying the Code of Conduct?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State confirm that appropriate public consultations will be carried out before any modifications are carried out to the Code of Conduct and Schedules?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Understanding the timeline for potential revisions will help stakeholders anticipate adjustments and plan accordingly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is on the scope of premises that are covered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The First and Second Schedules can be amended to vary the scope of qualifying leases covered by the Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The general power to exempt by order in the Gazette is less likely to attract scrutiny than amending the Schedules.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share under what circumstances might the Minister exercise its power to exempt specific persons or premises under section 32 instead of amending the Schedules?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have acted for both landlords and tenants.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In principle, Sir, I agree on the need for fair and more balanced lease negotiations between landlord and tenants of retail premises.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is especially so when tenants have spent tens of thousands of dollars renovating their premises and establishing their businesses at the rented premises.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Often, there is goodwill built up by tenants in respect of a particular location.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: First, I agree with this principle that a landlord should act reasonably and not have the power to predetermine the lease of premises unless there is a requirement for redevelopment works.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And if the landlord does predetermine the lease due to redevelopment works, then it is only right that the landlord should make some offer of compensation to the tenant for the costs of renovations incurred.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, Sir, I want to express some caution when Parliament is asked to legislate on matters which ought to be determined by market forces.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This was a similar principle made by Minister Indranee Rajah in February 2018 when she responded to my colleague, the hon Mr Murali Pillai, during his Adjournment Motion.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: She said, "In general, free market principles should apply." Sir, I am also concerned that the Code of Conduct is not a subsidiary legislation drawn up by the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) but by FTIC which has the right to propose modifications to the Code of Conduct.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Although members of FTIC are appointed by the Minister, in the event that, one day, more members of this FTIC are pro-tenants, then there is a risk that the recommendations in the Code of Conduct may tilt too much towards protection of a tenant who is not the owner of the property.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Landlords are typically owners of properties and they had paid hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars to buy real estate.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These property owners then part with possession of the premises to tenants who are given exclusive possession of the premises for the duration of the tenancy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And in many landlord-tenancy disputes, the greatest worry of the landlord is that they are unable to recover possession of the premises from a tenant in default of rental.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: By the time the landlord commences legal action to seek an order of possession, the arrears would have accumulated to a large amount.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hence, the starting point for most tenancy agreements is that they seek to protect the landlord to enable the landlord to recover possession of the premises whenever there is a breach of tenancy agreement.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of us in this House may not remember the Control of Rent Act – except Mr Murali – which was legislated after World War II to protect tenants against unscrupulous landlords during the housing shortage in the post-war years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, eventually, the Control of Rent Act was abolished and this was because it had outlived its purposes as there was no longer a housing shortage.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Further, at that point of time, rental control tenants had demanded exorbitant compensation before agreeing to vacate the rent-controlled premises.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And, Sir, I have acted for such tenants before the Tenants Compensation Board.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: During times when there is a shortage of retail space, usually landlords have a better bargaining position.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And we have had a relatively strong economy for many years and property prices remain strong.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, during times when there is a glut of retail space, tenants can and will make demands for better tenancy terms from the landlord.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They will moderate their tenancy terms in order to rent out their premises.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Otherwise, vacant premises are deemed to be a wasting resource to the landlord.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If there are many retail properties which are vacant, it may cause property prices to nosedive.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Members of this House who have lived through the Asian Financial Crisis in 1997 will know that a negative property market may eventually result in a recession because property owners cannot pay for their loan instalments and many property owners face financial ruin.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In fact, observers of the retail market will also know that not all retail spaces are in equal demand.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are some shopping malls where there are still many empty retail spaces as compared to a major shopping mall where there is huge demand for retail space due to better management of the mall.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, Sir, I would urge that we should consider allowing free market principles to set tenancy terms as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In respect of the Bill, I have a few queries for the Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As long as it can be proven by the landlord that the A&P charges are meant to promote the mall or the building, why does the Code of Conduct restrict the amount of A&P charge to be collected?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The setting of this rule would cause a landlord to simply refuse to conduct any A&P activities for the building or the mall if he is unable to raise A&P charges without cutting back on the amount of rental that he receives.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, if the total amount of rent cannot be changed, then he will simply not do any A&P activities because why would he want to cut his own rental?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Paragraph 4 of the Code of Conduct also provides for the landlord to pay compensation if there is predetermination of the lease.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is to avoid a situation whereby the tenant may have forgotten to keep or to submit records of their capex and thus be unable to substantiate their claim in the event that the landlord does predetermine the tenancy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Next, Sir, I want to speak about clause 2 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Clause 2 of the Bill provides for the law to be applied to all qualifying leases.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, would they be aware of the need to provide a certificate from the registered surveyor or the cap on the amount of security deposit?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I know many of these small landlords would have absolutely no clue where to find a registered surveyor because they have been renting out the place for so many years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Next, Part 4 of the Bill requires the landlord or tenant to settle disputes with an authorised dispute resolution body and that authorised dispute resolution body must then maintain a panel of mediators and a panel of adjudicators.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What if one party refuses to consent to the recoding of the settlement agreement?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And save for those concerns, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Despite the rise of online shopping and transactions, the retail shops in our neighbourhoods and shopping malls are still an invaluable part of our lives in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Bill is significant, as mentioned by some of our hon Members who have delivered their speeches, as it seeks to regulate the negotiation of private leases between landlords and tenants.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It represents an exception to Singapore's reluctance to interfere with the free market of private commercial transactions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It goes beyond the specific and temporary interventions that this House had passed during the height of the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Code was co-created by the retail industry landlord and tenant representatives through extensive discussions between June 2020 and March 2021.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That time period suggests that the Code was created in a context where COVID-19 had significantly affected retail businesses as footfall plunged during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are the principles in the Code suitable for permanent adoption going forward, especially as we leave the pandemic days behind us?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Clause 5 of the Bill, which introduces the Code into legislation, provides that the Code can only be modified with the Minister's approval.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister of State, would such a requirement introduce bureaucratic "red tape" that makes the Code less nimble and ready to adapt to changing market conditions?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And how many times has the Code been amended or revised since it was initially issued?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, Part A of the Code mandates landlords and tenants to "adopt a consensual approach to negotiate in good faith".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the passing of this Bill, is there now a legal duty to negotiate in good faith, even in the absence of an express contractual term?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that this is not the current state of the law.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Part D of the Code also requires a landlord to provide the tenant with a completed checklist indicating whether its draft lease agreement deviates or disapplies particular leasing principles under the Code.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I understand that the Code has already been voluntarily adopted by major private sector landlords like CapitaLand, CDL, Frasers and Keppel Land, I am concerned about the compliance readiness and costs to other relatively smaller landlords of retail premises, such as, for example, Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura (MUIS) or clan associations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Most significantly, there has been some concern over the Bill’s silence on the data transparency guidelines at Part C of the Code.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The tenant group Singapore Tenants United for Fairness (SGTuff) made a public call for landlords to be required to provide data on the footfall and average rental per square foot in their retail premises.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such data provides tenants with a more even playing field when negotiating shopping mall leases with building landlords, especially if the lease contemplates a gross turnover rent structure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the application of leasing principles set out at Part B of the Code, the Bill provides that this would only apply to a "qualifying lease".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Among other things, the lease would be one which is for at least one year, and any period for which the lease can be later extended or renewed is disregarded.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, the Code also provides that deviations for the first three principles are to be "on an exceptional basis".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Committee will maintain a register and record of permitted deviations under clause 7 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there room for the FTIC to interfere with these permitted deviations if they have been mutually agreed by the landlord and tenant in question?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
