text: I would also like to commend, Mr Speaker, the aim of a "low-cost and expedient" dispute resolution process for any non-compliance with leasing principles, through the introduction of mediation and adjudication processes at Part 4 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I look forward to seeing the rules, procedures and other details that will be established under clause 10 by the authorised dispute resolution body, which I understand will be the Singapore Mediation Centre (SMC).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, can the Minister of State clarify if there would be a stipulation equivalent to paragraph 3 of Part D of the Code of Conduct?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It says there that a landlord or tenant may escalate any non-compliance in the lease agreement to SMC "within 14 days of the signing of the lease agreement".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If yes, what is the consequence if the parties do not escalate the matter within 14 days of signing the lease agreement?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A bit of a technicality, but I thought it is good to clear this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are they barred from raising the issue from then on?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To keep the process "low-cost and expedient", will the mediation and adjudication be carried out without lawyers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also note that the prescribed mediation and adjudication process is only meant to cover a dispute over "non-compliance with a leasing principle in relation to their lease agreement".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If there are concurrently other disputes arising out of the lease agreement, I presume these will have to be referred to the Courts or to arbitration, depending on what the lease agreement provides.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In most longer-term leases, including those that are renewable for further periods, there are usually terms providing for a rent review exercise to "refresh" the rent payable after a certain period of time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This recognises that rent amounts are susceptible to market changes and fluctuations over time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Rent review is an area which is regulated in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The proposed legislation will help to level the playing field for tenants and landlords.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It will enhance fairness and transparency during the negotiation process and empower both parties to make informed decisions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill supports entrepreneurship by providing businesses with guidance and certainty.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can expect beneficial change for the whole community, not just the retail sector.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will be especially helpful for small business owners with limited means and information resources in their negotiations with landlords.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They form an important part of our communities, providing products and services catered to their customers’ specific needs in the housing estates.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will they also be able to benefit from this legislation and obtain access to the necessary information, which will be made available to the main tenants?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We want to continue to support these local businesses, some of which are quite unique, preserving our cultural heritage in the products and services rendered.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: More balanced bargaining power will maintain fair rates and would allow these entrepreneurs to prosper as well as to continue to contribute to the lively nature of the heartland districts.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While the Bill is undeniably a huge step forward in advancing the rights of tenants, more can be done.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One example is to go beyond sharing of sales data metrics by trade category before signing a lease.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: An open and transparent market will be beneficial to all stakeholders – landlords, tenants and consumers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):  The Bill and Code are important steps forward for the retail industry.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They will help to ensure a level playing field for tenants and landlords to negotiate lease agreements in openness and good faith.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They will also support entrepreneurship by providing businesses with guidance and certainty on the lease negotiation process and helping them make informed business decisions based on their commercial interests.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, many small landlords and tenants have long-term leasing agreements.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Based on their long-standing relationships, they may not regard lease negotiations in the same way as parties in commercial malls do.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, many HDB shops pay a lump-sum rent that is not tied to a specific psf rate, since they do not use psf as a benchmark to negotiate their rent.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some coffee shop operators sublet food stalls by verbal agreement.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, small businesses may not be sufficiently aware of the legislation to help them in their lease negotiations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What will the Ministry do to raise awareness of the Bill and Code and communicate their benefits more widely to the industry, especially among small businesses?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Government consider conducting townhalls and roadshows to reach out to these businesses?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What can be done to reassure small businesses which may be worried about compliance costs and whether their leases conform with the law?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can small tenants seek help to resolve disputes over non-compliance with the Bill and Code?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This unprecedented Bill is also a landmark for the Government, like what some Members have shared.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For the first time, we have tabled a Bill that mandates compliance with principles that are drawn from a Code that is developed by the industry, that is owned by the industry.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: It is because the industry and stakeholders recognised the need for this Code and the collective benefits that it can bring to the stakeholders of the retail sector that we are all here today for the final stage of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As Ms Jessica Tan pointed out, the Code does not set out to, nor does it intend to, solve every problem that tenants and landlords face in their lease negotiations.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: However, it is a critical first step that brings the industry together at the same table and steers it towards a positive direction for a brighter future.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: While the COVID-19 pandemic catalysed the beginnings of the Code, as Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Saktiandi Supaat said, the conduct and the spirit of negotiations, as well as the development of common leasing principles, will place businesses on a stronger foundation for the long run.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And to ensure its continued relevance, the Code will be a living document under the current Committee and then the FTIC’s stewardship, and updated from time to time to meet the industry's needs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Since the Code was first published in March 2021, it has been updated twice.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We are seeing the third version – Mr Louis Ng asked the question – in less than three years, three versions.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Louis Chua, Mr Leong Mun Wai, Ms See Jinli Jean in her maiden speech, and many Members have given their firm support, and I am very glad that the Bill addresses their concern about the imbalance of bargaining power for small companies in the retail leases.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I fully agree with Mr Murali Pillai that the Bill promotes equality, fairness and freedom to contract between leasing parties.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I also agree with Mr Don Wee, who has just spoken, that the Bill and the Code provide small businesses with guidance and certainty, and thus support entrepreneurship in general, by helping businesses understand their tenancy rights and make informed leasing decisions – knowing their tenancy rights as well as both sides knowing their obligations.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Above all, we are clear that by no means is this Bill signalling a shift in the Government’s position on free-market principles, the importance of which Mr Lim Biow Chuan had stressed in his very passionate speech earlier.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: On the contrary, the very reason that we are tabling this Bill is to promote greater transparency and a more vibrant and competitive retail scene to benefit Singaporeans and all consumers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As highlighted by Mr Murali Pillai in his passionate speech, the Government's underlying philosophy has always been, and still is, in the words of then-Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah in 2018, that "in general, free market principles should apply and the Government should only intervene when necessary." The Bill supports this approach.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: It does not seek to intervene in market outcomes and it does not seek to inadvertently distort competition or distort market forces at work.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Instead, it empowers the industry players in the retail sector to come together to identify, and to address, their key pain points by finding common ground.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The leasing principles under the Code are a result of very extensive deliberation between tenants and landlord representatives.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They represent the fine balance that both sides have struck.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The trust and partnership that tenants and landlords have forged in developing the Code together provide a firm foundation for widespread adoption by the industry.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: By mandating compliance with the Code, the Bill will enable both the tenants and the landlords to pursue their business interests more effectively and enhance the competitiveness of our retail scene in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: To formulate the Code, the Pro Tem Committee had spent months deliberating each of the leasing principles extensively.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Pro Tem Committee weighed the views of tenants, large and small, and landlords, large and small, and incorporated their feedback to come up with a set of common standards that apply to the industry.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Careful consideration was also given to ensure that the Code is not unduly onerous on any party.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The FTIC will certainly continue to drive the review of the Code under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Edward Chia had suggested amending specific leasing principles to further increase transparency in lease negotiations.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Edward Chia raised a point about electricity costs in his speech.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: He was concerned that while the Bill prohibits profiteering from the sale of electricity, tenants are charged for additional miscellaneous costs, such as "meter reading fees".

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Landlords on the En-bloc Contestability Scheme (ECS) will have to procure electricity contracts on behalf of all their tenants.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Then, the landlords are to pass tenants the electricity costs, as charged, without any mark-up.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Depending on the contract between the electricity retailer and the landlord, the electricity costs may include various components charged by the electricity retailer, such as fees for meter leasing and meter readings.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Under the ECS, the contract between, say, the electricity retailer with a mall, they will only measure the amount of electricity that the mall uses, but they will have to provide the individual meter to measure the tenants' usage.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, these are imposed by the electricity retailer.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is so that sub-meters can be installed for tenants and their electricity consumption can be tracked.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: There are also instances where the landlord is not on the ECS.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Those are cases where tenants would be able to choose from an array of electricity retailers of their choice from the open electricity market.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: It is thus not practical nor possible for the Code to comprehensively come up with different permutations to try to cover the different types of commercial arrangements for electricity.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As Ms Jessica Tan said in her speech, "We should not expect legislation to be the panacea for all issues." What is really important, as cited by many of the speakers today, is that details on costs are communicated transparently during the lease negotiation so that the tenant can make an informed decision whether to lease the premises.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Edward Chia also asked if the Government or FTIC could provide guidelines for parties renegotiating lease agreements due to material adverse change when a tenant cannot carry on its business because of events beyond its control.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Parties are encouraged to abide by the principles governing the conduct and the spirit of negotiations as set out in the Code and to negotiate leases in good faith while also considering the other party's legitimate interests.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As circumstances would differ for each lease, it is thus not feasible to issue guidelines for what would be commercial arrangements between the two parties.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Edward Chia and Mr Lim Biow Chuan raised some questions about advertising and promotion (A&P) and also service charges during the lease, which landlords are allowed to adjust, on the condition that their overall gross rent does not increase.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Again, this is to improve transparency and promote fair business practices so that there is certainty and predictability for retail tenants.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This condition has been set to prevent landlords from arbitrarily raising the gross rent after the agreement has been signed and to provide certainty to tenants on the rent that is payable during the lease term.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I wish to also clarify that the Code does not restrict the amount of A&P charges that a landlord may collect.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As Mr Lim Biow Chuan noted, the amount of A&P charges that is payable by the tenant is really a matter of negotiation between parties and continues to be so.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In addition, landlords are also encouraged to keep proper records and accounts of these charges to ensure accountability because when renewing the lease agreement, tenants and landlords may review and revise the charges based on prevailing market conditions.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In cases of non-compliance, parties can pursue recourse in the form of mediation and adjudication.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Don Wee and Mr Louis Chua asked if the data transparency principle in the Code can be further strengthened, such as by providing tenants with more information beyond sales data by trade category.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Allow me to share that the Pro Tem Committee had considered all these matters in deliberating on the data transparency requirement.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Pro Tem Committee ultimately landed on the position in the Code that Members see today to promote greater transparency and enable both tenants and landlords to make informed lease decisions while balancing both parties' interests.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The addition of two leasing principles, confidentiality and data transparency, really demonstrates how the Code is a living document which will continue to evolve to meet the industry's needs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: While I am not able to address all the questions that were raised by Members, especially those that are outside the purview of the Code and the Bill, I will certainly convey your feedback to the current Committee for their consideration, including Mr Lim Biow Chuan's suggestion for reminders to be sent for the declaration of the value of capex works.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the frequency of reviewing the Code and its guiding criteria.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat then enquired about rent review and if requiring the Minister's approval to amend the Code could make it less nimble.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I agree with both Mr Louis Ng and Mr Saktiandi Supaat that we will have to balance between providing flexibility and transparency and giving businesses certainty.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The current Committee considered the industry's feedback when it reviewed the Code and will continue to do so.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Under the Bill, MTI will also work with FTIC and ensure there is sufficient lead time for businesses to familiarise themselves with the latest updates on the Code and how the updated principles in the Code will be implemented before it comes into force.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Powers to vary the Schedules and to exempt specific entities are not uncommon in other Acts and I would like to assure the Member that MTI will exercise such powers under the Bill judiciously and only consider doing that in exceptional circumstances.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat observed, some parties may seek to escape compliance with the Bill by deliberately structuring their lease in multiple renewal periods of 11 months – that is actually quite painful.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: He was citing that as an example that some tenants or landlords may game it that way.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I wish to assure him that the intent is to cover the vast majority of retail leases and exempt those on short-term leases.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to assure him that if any party suspects that their lease terms are being deliberately shortened to circumvent compliance with the Code and the Bill, they can report to the FTIC such practices for going against the spirit of the Code.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked about the composition of the FTIC and cited there might be a risk of the balance of representation tilting towards either side.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: He noted the importance of this matter as the FTIC is responsible for maintaining and proposing changes to the Code.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We have chosen to do so as, one, we recognise the potential downsides of overregulating in the lease negotiation space, where market forces and commercial considerations should prevail.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Two, we do so because we recognise the benefits of having an industry-led body respond very nimbly and represent the industry aptly to changing needs in the fast-moving retail scene.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: To ensure accountability in the process and fair consideration of interests on both sides, the Bill requires FTIC members appointed by the Minister for Trade and Industry to represent the interests of both tenants and landlords and also requires the FTIC to seek the Minister's approval before amending the Code.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Edward Chia and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about the recourse available if landlords do not file declarations of permitted deviation after signing the lease agreement within the period to be prescribed in the Regulations.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: While the Bill only requires landlords to file any such declarations with the FTIC, tenants are encouraged to acknowledge these filings.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, they have to file it within that period, failing which, deviations on those three areas would be void and the default position in the Code would then apply.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is because it is not possible to prescribe a default rental formula in the Code or to void the rental formula term in that particular lease agreement as it is an essential element of the contract.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: On a related note, Mr Louis Ng asked about the consequences of non-compliance with leasing principles without a permitted deviation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Out of the 13 leasing principles, there are four leasing principles where, if both parties mutually agree, they can file a declaration of permitted deviation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And in such cases, if he is aware of any, the tenant can decline the lease agreement and, in fact, report the matter to FTIC.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: To answer Mr Saktiandi Supaat's question on the purpose of requiring parties to file declarations of permitted deviation with the FTIC, this is a good question.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: These requirements enable the FTIC to monitor industry trends in relation to the four leasing principles of exclusivity, sales performance, security deposit and rental formula, and then, to assess if there is a need to update the Code.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, as I said, this is a first step, it is a living document, we will continue to engage the industry to collect feedback but it has to be done in a way that all parties come to a consensus at the same table.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We keep talking about "large landlord" and "small tenants".

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, there are many, many permutations here and it is important for us to represent the interests of all possible scenarios.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I hear from some Members that the reason why there are permitted deviations in the four areas, is it because the landlord wins?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Interestingly, the tenants are the ones who may advocate for that flexibility.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Because if not, they will think that, in certain situations, it may be overly restrictive.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to address the query by Mr Leong Mun Wai.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For example, I understand in our engagements with the stakeholders – and as I said, there are large and small landlords, and large and small tenants – I will quote to Members two very interesting examples, which did not come to my mind before my engagement with them.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I will give Members one example – a shop selling bak kwa.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They shared that they may have most of their sales around the Lunar New Year period.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Of course, you may say, actually we eat bak kwa throughout the whole year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: But I think we will agree, we see the long queues one-and-a-half months before Lunar New Year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: They may actually enjoy a huge spike in their income during that period, rather than a steady income stream year-round, compared to other F&Bs, like say, a bubble tea shop.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, the bak kwa shop tenant may prefer a "whichever is higher" rental formula, which then will allow them to negotiate with the landlord to pay a lower baseline rent for most of the months, except for the few months leading up to Lunar New Year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I think we do see that in some shopping malls, where the sales during the year-end holiday or sales to those people who go to Australia during the June holidays can be a bit higher than other months.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, I just want us to think of other possible scenarios.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Basically, this is not just the landlord, also the tenant representatives who told us that they hope for a little bit of flexibility so that it does not encumber them, when they go into a lease negotiation for the retail premises.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As lease agreements are private contracts between willing parties, tenants and landlords should do their due diligence before signing a lease agreement, which is binding once signed.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Parties to the lease agreements are also responsible for ensuring compliance with the Code.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Tenants and landlords, after signing, it is their responsibility to also ensure that there is compliance, failing which, they can then proceed to alert FTIC and then, if need be, there is a dispute resolution body, which I will touch on later.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: If the FTIC receives complaints that a party regularly engages in practices or behaviours that are against the spirit or the requirements of the Code, it may seek further information from the parties and publicly highlight egregious or non-cooperative and non-compliant behaviour.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about the qualifications of the mediators and adjudicators.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The mediators will comprise both legally trained and non-legally trained individuals who must pass SMC's training programme with a distinction grade.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And all adjudicators have to be legally trained individuals.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is to ensure that they are able to address any legal implications in relation to non-compliance with the Code when rendering their decisions.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: While parties are free to hire their own legal representatives, it is not a requirement.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Here, we are trying to make sure that, in the situation of dispute, we are trying to offer a low-cost, expedient avenue.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Murali Pillai, in his speech, also asked about the adjudicator's power to address matters of non-compliance with leasing principles and whether the adjudicator can order both a variation of the lease as well as compensation to rectify the same matter of non-compliance.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This part is going to be quite technical, so please bear with me.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, this will only kick in during that period – at the front part of your lease agreement.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Currently, if you look at the Code – which is available at the URL www.ftic.org.sg, 39 pages long – compensation explicitly applies to three leasing principles in the Code relating to early termination of contracts.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In other cases of non-compliance where the leasing principle does not provide for recourse of compensation, the aggrieved party may wish to seek damages through independent civil redress, like what the Member cited.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked if the dispute resolution process under this Bill supersedes Court proceedings.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to assure them that it does not.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As I have said, we would want to do this because we want to provide the aggrieved party a low-cost and expedient avenue.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: It is not intended to override any other such redress.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Court would have the discretion, whether to hear or determine the matter or to grant a stay of proceedings, after considering all relevant circumstances.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Murali Pillai's last question concerns the scope to appeal the decisions of the adjudicator.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As I have shared, the dispute resolution framework under the Bill is intended to be a low-cost and expedient alternative to other forms of redress available to the parties.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Parties can only seek mediation or adjudication in relation to non-compliance with the leasing principles which have been clearly set out in the Code.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Thus, most cases before the adjudicator should be able to be determined in a relatively straightforward manner.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: (In Mandarin):  Mr Speaker, the Code of Conduct for Leasing of Retail Premises in Singapore, launched in March 2021, was spearheaded by the industry to promote fairer and more balanced lease negotiations between tenants and landlords.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We hope that the Bill will also support entrepreneurship, by helping businesses understand their tenancy rights and make informed leasing decisions.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This will set a strong foundation for a more vibrant and competitive retail scene in Singapore, which will benefit all consumers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: CapitaLand, a major landlord of commercial properties, shared that since adopting the Code, they have strengthened their relationship with their tenants and it has enabled them to work together to enhance the vibrancy of their malls and bring more exciting experiences to consumers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Don Wee and Mr Louis Chua asked how we can raise awareness of the Bill and Code among SMEs and address concerns over compliance costs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Lim Biow Chuan also expressed concerns on compliance readiness for smaller landlords.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I understand Members’ concerns and would like to assure them that we have refined the Code over a period of two years and we have tried to ensure right from the beginning that it is easy to understand and follow.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Government will work with FTIC, the Federation of Merchants’ Associations Singapore (FMAS) and Heartland Enterprise Centre Singapore (HECS) to conduct roadshows and seminars in the heartlands, especially from now to February next year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: He also asked whether they will be conducted in dialects.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, we will work closely with FTIC, FMAS and HECS to conduct a series of roadshows and seminars to educate heartland shops about the details of the Bill and Code.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Businesses can also approach HECS’ business advisors for one-on-one advice.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We are grateful to the TACs, including FMAS and the Restaurant Association of Singapore, for their ground-up efforts to introduce sector-specific lease agreement templates, checklists and other resources, which will bring more convenience to businesses.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: FTIC will continue to update the Code based on industry feedback.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For example, during our engagements in partnership with FMAS and HECS in the past two years, many heartland retailers gave feedback that the requirement to provide a surveyed floor plan certified by a registered surveyor for new leases would increase their leasing costs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: After considering the feedback, the current Committee decided that tenants and landlords can submit certified floor or building plans from relevant authorities by mutual agreement.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This shows that the Committee listens closely to the feedback from both tenants and landlords, large and small.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The alternative option is more convenient and less costly.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, I believe I have addressed the key issues that were raised by Members.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And as we can see from the last two-and-a-half hours of debate, the passionate speeches of the 10 Members, we have heard many different voices in the Chamber today.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: On one hand, while some Members think that the Code can go further to address imbalances in lease negotiations, others worry that it may go too far.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And some see the Bill as an exemplary example of our collaborative approach – "uniquely Singapore" – to problem-solving, while some caution that not all issues require the Government to step in and not all issues require the Government's intervention.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, as you can hear from the 10 speeches from the Members, the diversity of views held amongst the 10 speakers – I was reflecting.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: It truly reflects the extensive and spirited discussions that have taken place these two years in the industry, between the large and small landlords and the large and small tenants.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I am very heartened that all 10 Members affirmed the importance of the Code and the need for the Bill to ensure widespread adoption.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This will allow new and current players to navigate the market more adroitly and adapt to disruptions with greater resilience.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I am confident that by ensuring fair and balanced lease negotiations, the Bill will strengthen the foundations of the retail market.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The FTIC will also be a positive driving force in finetuning the Code and bringing stakeholders together to push the industry to greater heights.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And I trust that with the support of the House today and the retail industry for this Bill and the Code, we will place the retail sector on solid ground for future growth and greater potential.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any clarifications for Minister of State Low?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I call the Deputy Leader, next Wednesday, we celebrate our country's 58th birthday.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, let me wish everyone a happy National Day in advance.
